sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Where share-related items appear in the balance sheet
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Share capital
(B) Securities Premium
(C) Calls in arrears
(D) Unpaid dividend

List-II (Presentation)
(I) Shareholders' funds — Share capital
(II) Shareholders' funds — Reserves and surplus
(III) Deducted from called-up capital in the notes
(IV) Current liabilities — Other current liabilities
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Share capital is the first item of shareholders' funds (I).
(B) Securities Premium is a reserve (II).
(C) Calls in arrears reduce called-up capital in the notes (III).
(D) Declared but unpaid dividend is owed to shareholders → other current liabilities (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps capital and premium; (B) swaps premium and arrears; (C) swaps capital and unpaid dividend.
Key point: Equity items under shareholders' funds; amounts owed under liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debenture interest — a charge even in a loss year
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Interest on debentures is debited to the Statement of Profit and Loss as a finance cost even in a year in which the company incurs a loss.
Reason (R): Interest on debentures is a charge against profit, not an appropriation of profit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Debenture holders are lenders, and the company is legally bound to pay them interest. Because the interest is a charge (R), it is recorded as a finance cost whatever the result for the year (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Interest (charge) is paid regardless; dividend (appropriation) depends on profits.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings at a flat rate (rate not per annum)
questions.question: The deed of a firm says: 'Interest on drawings will be charged at 6%' — the words 'per annum' are not used. Partner Gita's drawings during the year were ₹40,000, made on various dates. The interest on her drawings is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹2,400
Why: When the rate is stated without 'per annum', it is treated as a FLAT rate, charged on the total drawings regardless of the time for which they were outstanding.
Step 1: Interest = ₹40,000 × 6% = ₹2,400
Common mistake: Applying the average period of 6 months gives ₹1,200 (A). 3 months gives ₹600 (C). 9 months gives ₹1,800 (D).
Key point: '6% p.a.' → time-based; '6%' → flat.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Fixed capital method — which account records which item
questions.question:
The partners maintain fixed capitals. Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Additional capital introduced
(B) Interest on capital
(C) Drawings
(D) Permanent withdrawal of capital

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Credited to the Capital Account
(II) Credited to the Current Account
(III) Debited to the Current Account
(IV) Debited to the Capital Account
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Only PERMANENT changes in capital pass through the Capital Account — additions are credited (I) and permanent withdrawals debited (IV). Routine items go to the Current Account: interest on capital is credited (II) and drawings are debited (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps additional capital and interest on capital; (C) swaps interest and drawings; (D) swaps the two permanent items.
Key point: Permanent → Capital A/c; recurring → Current A/c.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Final payment to a partner who took over a liability and had a debit current account
questions.question: On dissolution, partner Bhanu has a capital of ₹30,000 and a DEBIT balance of ₹4,000 in his Current Account. He agrees to take over creditors of ₹10,000, and his share of the loss on realisation is ₹6,000. The cash paid to Bhanu in final settlement is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹30,000
Step 1: Capital ₹30,000, less the current account debit balance ₹4,000 = ₹26,000
Step 2: Add creditors taken over (Realisation A/c Dr.; To Bhanu's Capital A/c) = +₹10,000
Step 3: Less share of realisation loss = −₹6,000
Step 4: Cash paid = ₹30,000
Common mistake: Adding the current account debit gives ₹38,000 (A). Deducting the liability taken over gives ₹10,000 (B). Ignoring the loss gives ₹36,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Rights issue — meaning
questions.question: Delta Ltd. offers new shares to its existing shareholders in proportion to their present holdings, at a stated price. This is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Rights issue
Why: Under Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013, further shares may be offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings — a rights issue. Shareholders may accept, renounce or decline the offer.
Why not the others:
(A) Bonus shares are free.
(B) A private placement is made to a select group.
(C) An ESOP is for employees.
Key point: Existing holders + proportionate offer + price = rights issue.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Minimum subscription not received — refund of all application money
questions.question: Comet Ltd. offered 1,00,000 shares, with ₹3 per share payable on application. It received applications for only 85,000 shares. Applying the minimum subscription rule, the company must:
options: A) Refund ₹2,55,000 and allot no shares
B) Allot 85,000 shares and refund nothing
D) Allot 90,000 shares by calling on the directors to subscribe ₹30,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Refund ₹2,55,000 and allot no shares
Step 1: Minimum subscription = 90% of 1,00,000 = 90,000 shares
Step 2: Applications (85,000) fall short, so no allotment can be made
Step 3: All application money must be refunded = 85,000 × ₹3 = ₹2,55,000
Common mistake: (B) ignores the minimum subscription rule. (C) refunds only the shortfall (15,000 × ₹3). (D) describes no legal remedy.
Key point: Below 90% → refund everything; no partial allotment.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — entry for premium brought in cash
questions.question: Sita is admitted into the firm of Ravi and Mohan. She brings ₹50,000 as capital and ₹10,000 as her share of goodwill, both in cash. The entry for the goodwill amount is:
options: A) Cash A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Sita's Capital A/c ₹10,000
B) Cash A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Premium for Goodwill A/c ₹10,000
C) Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Cash A/c ₹10,000
D) Sita's Capital A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Premium for Goodwill A/c ₹10,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cash A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To Premium for Goodwill A/c ₹10,000
Why: Cash received for goodwill is first credited to Premium for Goodwill A/c, which is then transferred to the sacrificing partners (Ravi and Mohan).
Why not the others:
(A) The premium is not Sita's capital.
(C) raises a Goodwill Account, which is not done.
(D) is used when the premium is NOT brought in cash.
Key point: Premium in cash → Cash Dr.; To Premium for Goodwill → sacrificing partners.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Commission to partners — rules
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about commission payable to a partner:
(A) It may be calculated on the profit before charging the commission or after charging it.
(B) It is allowed only if the partnership deed provides for it.
(C) It is an appropriation of profit.
(D) When the deed is silent, it is allowed at 6% of the profit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The deed may fix commission on profit before or after charging it (A). Commission exists only if agreed (B), and it is debited to the P&L Appropriation Account (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — under Section 13, no partner is entitled to any remuneration (salary or commission) when the deed is silent. The 6% rule applies only to interest on partners' loans. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Deed silent → no salary, no commission, no interest on capital.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on calls in arrears at the rate fixed by the Articles
questions.question: A company's Articles provide for interest on calls in arrears at 8% p.a. A shareholder paid a call of ₹4,000, which was due on 1 October 2026, only on 31 December 2026. The interest recoverable from him is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹80
Step 1: Period = 1 October to 31 December = 3 months
Step 2: Interest = ₹4,000 × 8% × 3/12 = ₹80
Common mistake: Using the Table F rate of 10% gives ₹100 (A) — but the company's own Articles fix 8%. A full year gives ₹320 (C). Using 12% gives ₹120 (D).
Key point: Articles' rate first; Table F applies only if the company has adopted it.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Bank loan repaid with interest on dissolution
questions.question: On dissolution, the firm's bank loan of ₹50,000 (already transferred to the Realisation Account) was repaid together with ₹2,000 of interest due on it. The amount debited to the Realisation Account for this payment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹52,000
Why: The loan was credited to the Realisation Account at ₹50,000. The full cash paid, including interest, is debited: Realisation A/c Dr. ₹52,000; To Cash A/c ₹52,000. The extra ₹2,000 increases the realisation loss.
Common mistake: Ignoring the interest gives ₹50,000 (A). ₹2,000 (C) is only the interest. Subtracting the interest gives ₹48,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: No deed — profits shared equally despite unequal capitals
questions.question: Mohan contributed ₹5,00,000 and Sohan ₹1,00,000 to a business they run together, but they never made a partnership agreement on profit sharing. This year's profit is ₹60,000. Their shares will be:
options: D) Whatever Mohan, as the larger contributor, decides
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹30,000 each
Why: Under Section 13(b) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, when there is no agreement, partners share profits EQUALLY, whatever their capital contributions.
Why not the others: (B) uses the capital ratio, which applies only if agreed. (C) has no basis. (D) No partner can decide alone.
Key point: No agreement → equal sharing; capital ratio needs an agreement.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profit sharing in two tiers
questions.question: Ajay and Bina agree that the first ₹1,00,000 of profit each year will be shared equally, and any profit above ₹1,00,000 in the ratio 3 : 2. This year's profit is ₹1,60,000. Ajay's share is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹86,000
Step 1: First ₹1,00,000 equally → Ajay ₹50,000
Step 2: Excess ₹60,000 in 3 : 2 → Ajay ₹36,000
Step 3: Ajay's total = ₹86,000 (Bina ₹74,000)
Common mistake: Applying 3 : 2 to the whole profit gives ₹96,000 (A). Sharing it all equally gives ₹80,000 (B). ₹74,000 (D) is Bina's share.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Bearer debentures
questions.question: Debentures that can be transferred simply by handing them over, without any registration of the transfer, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bearer debentures
Why: Bearer debentures are negotiable instruments; whoever holds them receives the interest and the redemption amount, and transfer is by mere delivery.
Why not the others:
(B) Registered debentures need a transfer deed and registration.
(C) Security refers to a charge on assets.
(D) Conversion refers to the right to become shares.
Key point: Bearer → delivery; registered → transfer deed.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: New ratio when the new partner's share comes from old partners in a given ratio
questions.question: Ashwin and Bindu share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. Chandni is admitted for a 3/10th share, which she acquires from Ashwin and Bindu in the ratio 2 : 1. The new profit-sharing ratio of Ashwin, Bindu and Chandni is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4 : 3 : 3
Step 1: Ashwin gives 3/10 × 2/3 = 2/10; Bindu gives 3/10 × 1/3 = 1/10
Step 2: Ashwin = 6/10 − 2/10 = 4/10; Bindu = 4/10 − 1/10 = 3/10; Chandni = 3/10
Step 3: New ratio = 4 : 3 : 3
Common mistake: 3 : 2 : 3 (B) does not reduce the old shares. Assuming sacrifice in the old ratio 3 : 2 gives 21 : 14 : 15 (C). 2 : 2 : 1 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Closing the Realisation Account
questions.question: After all assets have been realised and all outside liabilities paid, the balance of the Realisation Account is transferred to:
options: C) Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
D) Partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
Why: The balance is the profit or loss on realisation, which belongs to the partners and is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Why not the others: (A) Cash settles capitals later. (B) and (C) are not used on dissolution.
Key point: Realisation profit or loss → partners' capitals, profit-sharing ratio.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Premium payable with a call — amount credited to Securities Premium
questions.question: Neon Ltd. issued 10,000 shares of ₹10 each at ₹12. The premium of ₹2 per share was payable with the first call. When the call was made, the holders of 500 shares failed to pay it. The amount credited to Securities Premium when the call was made is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹20,000
Why: The premium is credited when the call is MADE (Share First Call A/c Dr.; To Share Capital; To Securities Premium), not when it is received.
Step 1: Premium credited = 10,000 × ₹2 = ₹20,000
Common mistake: Deducting the defaulters gives ₹19,000 (A) — non-payment is recorded later in Calls in Arrears. ₹1,000 (B) is the defaulters' premium. ₹24,000 (C) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Total cash received over the life of forfeited and re-issued shares
questions.question: A company forfeited 1,000 shares of ₹10 each after their original holder had paid ₹6 per share. It later re-issued all of them at ₹9 per share as fully paid. The total cash the company received on these 1,000 shares, from both holders together, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹15,000
Step 1: From the original holder = 1,000 × ₹6 = ₹6,000
Step 2: From the new holder = 1,000 × ₹9 = ₹9,000
Step 3: Total = ₹15,000 (for share capital of ₹10,000 — the extra ₹5,000 is the capital profit: forfeited ₹6,000 − discount ₹1,000 → Capital Reserve)
Common mistake: ₹10,000 (A) is the face value. ₹9,000 (B) and ₹6,000 (C) each count only one holder.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Commission after charging interest on capital, salary and the commission itself
questions.question: A firm's profit before interest on capital, salary and commission is ₹2,50,000. Interest on capital totals ₹20,000 and partner Rekha's salary is ₹10,000. Partner Mohan's commission is 10% of the profit remaining after charging interest on capital, the salary AND his commission. Mohan's commission is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹20,000
Step 1: Profit after interest on capital and salary = ₹2,50,000 − ₹20,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹2,20,000
Step 2: Commission after charging itself = ₹2,20,000 × 10/110 = ₹20,000
Step 3: Check: divisible profit = ₹2,00,000, and 10% of it = ₹20,000 ✔
Common mistake: 10% of ₹2,20,000 gives ₹22,000 (A). 10% of ₹2,50,000 gives ₹25,000 (C). 10/110 of ₹2,50,000 gives ₹22,727 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital as a charge in a year with insufficient profit
questions.question: The deed of Arun and Barun treats interest on capital as a CHARGE against profit. The profit before interest on capital is ₹20,000. Interest on capital is ₹18,000 for Arun and ₹12,000 for Barun, and they share profits and losses in the ratio 3 : 2. The net effect of these items on Arun's Current Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Credit of ₹12,000
Step 1: As a charge, the full interest of ₹30,000 is allowed even though the profit is only ₹20,000
Step 2: Result after interest = ₹20,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹10,000 LOSS, shared 3 : 2 → Arun's share of loss = ₹6,000
Step 3: Arun's net = +₹18,000 − ₹6,000 = ₹12,000 credit
Common mistake: Ignoring the loss gives ₹18,000 (A). ₹6,000 (B) is only his share of the loss. Adding the loss gives ₹24,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death of a partner — rights of the executor
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the death of a partner:
(A) The executor is entitled to the deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death.
(B) Interest on capital up to the date of death is allowed if the deed provides for it.
(C) The gaining partners compensate for the deceased partner's share of goodwill.
(D) The executor automatically becomes a partner in place of the deceased partner.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The deceased partner's estate receives everything he was entitled to up to the date of death — his share of profit (A), interest on capital if agreed (B), and his share of goodwill from the gaining partners (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — partnership is a personal relationship; an executor does not become a partner unless all the partners agree to admit him. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: The executor is a creditor for the amount due, not a partner.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Sacrificing ratio may differ from the old ratio
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On admission, the sacrificing ratio of the old partners need not be the same as their old profit-sharing ratio.
Reason (R): The new partner may acquire his share from the old partners in any proportion they agree upon.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: If the new partner takes his share in the old ratio, the sacrificing ratio equals the old ratio. But the partners may agree otherwise — for example, all of it from one partner (R) — and then the sacrificing ratio differs (A).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Compute sacrifice as Old − New; never assume it.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — settlement partly by an asset, partly in cash, balance as loan
questions.question: After all adjustments, ₹80,000 is due to Kiran, a retiring partner. She takes over the firm's car at its agreed value of ₹30,000 and is paid ₹20,000 in cash; the balance is to remain as a loan to the firm. The amount transferred to Kiran's Loan Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹30,000
Step 1: Amount due = ₹80,000
Step 2: Less car taken over (Kiran's Capital A/c Dr.; To Car A/c) = ₹30,000
Step 3: Less cash paid = ₹20,000
Step 4: Balance to loan = ₹30,000
Common mistake: Deducting only the car gives ₹50,000 (A). Deducting only the cash gives ₹60,000 (B). ₹80,000 (D) ignores both settlements.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Discount on re-issue of forfeited shares — account debited
questions.question: When forfeited shares are re-issued at a discount, the discount allowed is debited to the:
options: D) Statement of Profit and Loss
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Share Forfeiture Account
Why: The discount is met out of the amount already forfeited on those shares: Bank A/c Dr.; Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. (discount); To Share Capital A/c.
Why not the others:
(A) Securities Premium is not used for this.
(B) Capital Reserve receives only the SURPLUS left after re-issue.
(D) It is not a revenue expense.
Key point: The discount on re-issue can never exceed the forfeited amount.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture and re-issue — order of events
questions.question:
Arrange the following events relating to a shareholder's default in the correct order:
(A) Re-issue of the forfeited shares
(B) Non-payment of the call by the shareholder
(C) Forfeiture of the shares
(D) Transfer of the surplus on re-issued shares to Capital Reserve
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (C), (A), (D)
Why: Default comes first (B); after due notice the shares are forfeited (C); the forfeited shares may then be re-issued (A); and only after re-issue is the surplus on those shares transferred to Capital Reserve (D).
Why not the others: (A) forfeits before any default. (C) re-issues before forfeiting. (D) re-issues first.
Key point: Default → forfeit → re-issue → Capital Reserve.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Preference shares versus equity shares
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Preference shareholders receive their dividend before equity shareholders.
(B) Equity shareholders have voting rights on all resolutions.
(C) On winding up, preference capital is repaid before equity capital.
(D) Preference shareholders always have voting rights on all resolutions.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Preference shares carry priority in dividend (A) and in repayment of capital (C), while equity shareholders carry full voting rights (B).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — under Section 47, preference shareholders normally vote only on resolutions that directly affect their rights (or when their dividend remains unpaid for a specified period). Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Preference → priority; equity → control.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Shares payable in full on application — refund of excess
questions.question: Sun Ltd. offered 10,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹5, the whole ₹15 being payable with the application. It received applications for 12,000 shares and rejected the excess applications. The amount refunded is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹30,000
Step 1: Excess applications = 12,000 − 10,000 = 2,000 shares
Step 2: Refund = 2,000 × ₹15 = ₹30,000
Step 3: For the 10,000 allotted shares: Share Application A/c Dr. ₹1,50,000; To Share Capital ₹1,00,000; To Securities Premium ₹50,000
Common mistake: Refunding only the capital part (₹10) gives ₹20,000 (A). Refunding only the premium part gives ₹10,000 (B). ₹1,80,000 (D) is the total application money received.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — category-wise pro-rata allotment and refund to one applicant
questions.question: Applications for a share issue were divided into two categories: Category I applied for 20,000 shares and was allotted 10,000; Category II applied for 15,000 shares and was allotted 5,000, each on a pro-rata basis within its category. Application money was ₹3 and allotment money ₹4 per share; excess application money was adjusted towards allotment and any surplus refunded. Mr X, in Category II, applied for 600 shares. The amount refunded to him is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹400
Step 1: Category II allotment ratio = 5,000 ÷ 15,000 = 1/3 → Mr X gets 600 × 1/3 = 200 shares
Step 2: Application money paid = 600 × ₹3 = ₹1,800; required for 200 shares = ₹600 → excess ₹1,200
Step 3: Allotment due = 200 × ₹4 = ₹800, met from the excess
Step 4: Refund = ₹1,200 − ₹800 = ₹400
Common mistake: Refunding the whole excess gives ₹1,200 (A). ₹800 (C) is the amount adjusted. Assuming the excess is fully used gives Nil (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profit sharing — one partner's fixed share, others in a ratio
questions.question: Under their deed, Asha gets 1/4th of the firm's profit, and Bimal and Charu share the remainder in the ratio 3 : 2. The firm's profit is ₹1,00,000. Bimal's share is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹45,000
Step 1: Remainder after Asha = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4
Step 2: Bimal = 3/4 × 3/5 = 9/20; Charu = 3/4 × 2/5 = 6/20; Asha = 5/20
Step 3: Bimal's share = ₹1,00,000 × 9/20 = ₹45,000
Common mistake: Taking 3/5 of the whole profit gives ₹60,000 (A). ₹30,000 (B) is Charu's share. ₹37,500 (D) splits the remainder equally.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — super profit from the actual rate of return
questions.question: A firm employs capital of ₹4,00,000 and earns a return of 15% on it, while the normal rate of return in the industry is 10%. Goodwill is valued at three years' purchase of super profit. Its value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹60,000
Step 1: Actual profit = 15% × ₹4,00,000 = ₹60,000
Step 2: Normal profit = 10% × ₹4,00,000 = ₹40,000
Step 3: Super profit = ₹20,000 → Goodwill = ₹20,000 × 3 = ₹60,000
Common mistake: Three years' purchase of actual profit gives ₹1,80,000 (A). ₹20,000 (B) is the super profit. Three years of normal profit gives ₹1,20,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Contingent liability (bill discounted) materialising on dissolution
questions.question: At the time of dissolution, bills of ₹15,000 that had been discounted with the bank were still running. Later, one bill of ₹4,000 was dishonoured and the firm had to pay the bank. The entry for this payment is:
options: A) No entry, because it was a contingent liability
B) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000
C) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Cash A/c ₹15,000
D) Bills Receivable A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To Cash A/c ₹4,000
Why: A contingent liability is not in the books, so it is not transferred to the Realisation Account. When part of it actually becomes payable and is paid, that payment is a realisation loss, debited to the Realisation Account.
Why not the others:
(A) Once paid, it must be recorded.
(C) Only the ₹4,000 actually paid is recorded.
(D) The firm is closing its books, so no new asset account is opened.
Key point: Contingent liability that materialises → treat it like an unrecorded liability paid.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution — basic rules
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the accounts on dissolution:
(A) If goodwill is sold, the amount is credited to the Realisation Account.
(B) Partners' loans are paid after outside creditors.
(C) Realisation expenses borne by the firm are debited to the Realisation Account.
(D) Profit on realisation is shared in the ratio of the partners' capitals.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: All realisation proceeds go to the credit of the Realisation Account (A); Section 48 places partners' loans after outsiders (B); and expenses paid by the firm are realisation costs (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — profit or loss on realisation is shared in the PROFIT-SHARING ratio, not the capital ratio (unless the two happen to be the same). Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Realisation profit or loss → profit-sharing ratio.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — retiring share taken by one partner only
questions.question: Ajit, Bharat and Chandra share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Bharat retires, and his entire share is taken over by Chandra. The new profit-sharing ratio of Ajit and Chandra is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1 : 1
Step 1: Ajit = 3/6 (unchanged)
Step 2: Chandra = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6
Step 3: New ratio = 3 : 3 = 1 : 1
Common mistake: 3 : 1 (A) is the old ratio of Ajit and Chandra. 3 : 2 (C) treats Bharat's share as Ajit's. 2 : 1 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Memorandum Revaluation Account on admission — net effect on the new partner
questions.question: Asif and Bela share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. They admit Charu, and the new ratio is 2 : 2 : 1. The revaluation shows a profit of ₹25,000, but the partners decide to keep the old book values and to use a Memorandum Revaluation Account. The net effect on Charu's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Debit of ₹5,000
Step 1: First part (old ratio 3 : 2): Asif +₹15,000; Bela +₹10,000
Step 2: Second part reverses the profit in the NEW ratio 2 : 2 : 1: Asif −₹10,000; Bela −₹10,000; Charu −₹5,000
Step 3: Net: Asif +₹5,000; Bela nil; Charu −₹5,000 → Charu's Capital is debited ₹5,000
Common mistake: Reversing the sign gives (A). Thinking a new partner is unaffected gives Nil (B). Using 2/5 of the profit gives ₹10,000 (C).
Key point: The new partner pays for his share of the unrecorded gain.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — amount credited to the executor with reserve, revaluation loss and goodwill
questions.question: Dhruv, who had a 1/3rd share, died on 30 June 2026. His capital was ₹60,000. The firm had a General Reserve of ₹18,000; revaluation showed a LOSS of ₹6,000; the firm's goodwill was valued at ₹54,000; and his share of profit up to the date of death was ₹4,000. The amount transferred to his Executor's Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹86,000
Step 1: Capital ₹60,000 + reserve (1/3 × ₹18,000) ₹6,000 = ₹66,000
Step 2: Less revaluation loss (1/3 × ₹6,000) = −₹2,000
Step 3: Add goodwill (1/3 × ₹54,000) ₹18,000 + profit ₹4,000
Step 4: Total = 66,000 − 2,000 + 18,000 + 4,000 = ₹86,000
Common mistake: Treating the revaluation loss as a gain gives ₹90,000 (A). Ignoring goodwill gives ₹68,000 (B). Ignoring the profit to death gives ₹82,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — new partner's share of goodwill (premium in kind)
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Akhil and Bhavna share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. After revaluation and the distribution of reserves, their capitals are ₹1,80,000 and ₹1,20,000. On 1 April 2026 they admit Chetna for a 1/4th share; Akhil and Bhavna will share the remaining profit in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Instead of cash, Chetna brings machinery worth ₹50,000 and stock worth ₹30,000, together with ₹20,000 in cash. Out of the total value she brings, her share of goodwill is treated as premium and the rest as her capital. The old partners' capitals are then to be made proportionate to Chetna's capital, in the new profit-sharing ratio, by transfers to or from their Current Accounts.

Question: Chetna's share of goodwill, treated as premium, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹30,000
Step 1: Chetna's share = 1/4
Step 2: Premium = ₹1,20,000 × 1/4 = ₹30,000
Common mistake: Using 1/5 gives ₹24,000 (B). ₹1,20,000 (C) is the firm's goodwill. ₹20,000 (D) is the cash she brings, not her goodwill share.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — capital credited when assets are brought in kind
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Akhil and Bhavna share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. After revaluation and the distribution of reserves, their capitals are ₹1,80,000 and ₹1,20,000. On 1 April 2026 they admit Chetna for a 1/4th share; Akhil and Bhavna will share the remaining profit in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Instead of cash, Chetna brings machinery worth ₹50,000 and stock worth ₹30,000, together with ₹20,000 in cash. Out of the total value she brings, her share of goodwill is treated as premium and the rest as her capital. The old partners' capitals are then to be made proportionate to Chetna's capital, in the new profit-sharing ratio, by transfers to or from their Current Accounts.

Question: The amount credited to Chetna's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹70,000
Step 1: Total value brought = Machinery ₹50,000 + Stock ₹30,000 + Cash ₹20,000 = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Less premium for goodwill = ₹30,000
Step 3: Capital = ₹70,000
Entry: Machinery A/c Dr. ₹50,000; Stock A/c Dr. ₹30,000; Cash A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To Chetna's Capital A/c ₹70,000; To Premium for Goodwill A/c ₹30,000
Common mistake: Crediting the whole ₹1,00,000 to capital gives (A). ₹80,000 (C) counts only the assets in kind. ₹50,000 (D) counts only the machinery.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — new ratio when old partners keep their old ratio
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Akhil and Bhavna share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. After revaluation and the distribution of reserves, their capitals are ₹1,80,000 and ₹1,20,000. On 1 April 2026 they admit Chetna for a 1/4th share; Akhil and Bhavna will share the remaining profit in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Instead of cash, Chetna brings machinery worth ₹50,000 and stock worth ₹30,000, together with ₹20,000 in cash. Out of the total value she brings, her share of goodwill is treated as premium and the rest as her capital. The old partners' capitals are then to be made proportionate to Chetna's capital, in the new profit-sharing ratio, by transfers to or from their Current Accounts.

Question: The new profit-sharing ratio of Akhil, Bhavna and Chetna is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9 : 6 : 5
Step 1: Remaining share = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4
Step 2: Akhil = 3/4 × 3/5 = 9/20; Bhavna = 3/4 × 2/5 = 6/20; Chetna = 5/20
Step 3: New ratio = 9 : 6 : 5
Common mistake: 3 : 2 : 1 (A) gives Chetna 1/6. 3 : 2 : 5 (B) has no basis. 12 : 8 : 5 (C) gives Chetna 1/5.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — old partner's capital proportionate to the new partner's capital
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Akhil and Bhavna share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. After revaluation and the distribution of reserves, their capitals are ₹1,80,000 and ₹1,20,000. On 1 April 2026 they admit Chetna for a 1/4th share; Akhil and Bhavna will share the remaining profit in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Instead of cash, Chetna brings machinery worth ₹50,000 and stock worth ₹30,000, together with ₹20,000 in cash. Out of the total value she brings, her share of goodwill is treated as premium and the rest as her capital. The old partners' capitals are then to be made proportionate to Chetna's capital, in the new profit-sharing ratio, by transfers to or from their Current Accounts.

Question: On the basis of Chetna's capital, Akhil's capital in the new firm should be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,26,000
Step 1: Chetna's capital ₹70,000 is for a 1/4 share → total capital of the new firm = ₹70,000 × 4 = ₹2,80,000
Step 2: Akhil's required capital = ₹2,80,000 × 9/20 = ₹1,26,000
Common mistake: ₹1,98,000 (A) is Akhil's actual capital after the premium (1,80,000 + 18,000). Taking 3/5 of ₹2,80,000 gives ₹1,68,000 (B). Taking 3/4 gives ₹2,10,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — surplus capital transferred to an old partner's Current Account
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Akhil and Bhavna share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. After revaluation and the distribution of reserves, their capitals are ₹1,80,000 and ₹1,20,000. On 1 April 2026 they admit Chetna for a 1/4th share; Akhil and Bhavna will share the remaining profit in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Instead of cash, Chetna brings machinery worth ₹50,000 and stock worth ₹30,000, together with ₹20,000 in cash. Out of the total value she brings, her share of goodwill is treated as premium and the rest as her capital. The old partners' capitals are then to be made proportionate to Chetna's capital, in the new profit-sharing ratio, by transfers to or from their Current Accounts.

Question: The amount transferred from Bhavna's Capital Account to her Current Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹48,000
Step 1: Bhavna's share of the premium (2/5 of ₹30,000) = ₹12,000 → actual capital = ₹1,20,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹1,32,000
Step 2: Required capital = ₹2,80,000 × 6/20 = ₹84,000
Step 3: Surplus = ₹1,32,000 − ₹84,000 = ₹48,000 → Bhavna's Capital A/c Dr.; To Bhavna's Current A/c
Common mistake: Ignoring her share of the premium gives ₹36,000 (B). ₹12,000 (C) is only her share of the premium. ₹60,000 (D) has no basis.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Operating profit ratio — removing non-operating items
questions.question: A company's revenue from operations is ₹8,00,000 and its net profit (before tax) is ₹1,20,000. This profit includes a profit of ₹10,000 on the sale of an asset and interest received of ₹6,000, and it is after charging interest paid of ₹8,000. The operating profit ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 14%
Step 1: Operating profit = 1,20,000 − 10,000 − 6,000 (non-operating incomes) + 8,000 (non-operating expense) = ₹1,12,000
Step 2: Operating profit ratio = ₹1,12,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 × 100 = 14%
Common mistake: Using net profit gives 15% (A). Deducting the interest paid instead of adding it back gives 12% (B). Adding back the interest but not removing the incomes gives 16% (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Proprietary ratio after redeeming debentures in cash
questions.question: A company's total assets are ₹10,00,000, financed by shareholders' funds of ₹6,00,000, debentures of ₹2,50,000 and current liabilities of ₹1,50,000. It then redeems debentures of ₹1,00,000 by paying cash. Its proprietary ratio after the redemption is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.67 : 1
Step 1: After redemption: total assets = ₹10,00,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹9,00,000; shareholders' funds unchanged at ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Proprietary ratio = ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹9,00,000 = 0.67 : 1
Common mistake: 0.6 : 1 (A) is the ratio before redemption. 0.75 : 1 (B) and 0.5 : 1 (C) have no basis in the data.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Schedule III — long-term borrowings
questions.question: Which of the following is shown under 'Long-term borrowings' in a company's balance sheet?
options: B) Term loan from a bank repayable after three years
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Term loan from a bank repayable after three years
Why: Borrowings repayable after more than twelve months (beyond the operating cycle) are non-current — long-term borrowings.
Why not the others:
(A) An overdraft is a short-term borrowing.
(C) Trade payables are current liabilities.
(D) Calls in advance are other current liabilities.
Key point: Repayable after 12 months → long-term borrowings.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — starting from profit after tax
questions.question: A company's profit after tax is ₹1,26,000, after a provision for tax of ₹54,000. Depreciation was ₹20,000, a loss of ₹4,000 arose on the sale of furniture, and interest on debentures of ₹12,000 was charged. Inventory increased by ₹15,000 and creditors increased by ₹9,000. Income tax actually paid was ₹50,000. Net cash from operating activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,60,000
Step 1: Profit before tax = ₹1,26,000 + ₹54,000 = ₹1,80,000
Step 2: Add depreciation ₹20,000, loss on sale ₹4,000 and interest on debentures ₹12,000 (a financing item) → ₹2,16,000
Step 3: Working capital: −15,000 + 9,000 → ₹2,10,000
Step 4: Less tax paid ₹50,000 → ₹1,60,000
Common mistake: Not adding back the debenture interest gives ₹1,48,000 (A). Deducting the provision instead of the tax paid gives ₹1,56,000 (B). Starting from profit after tax gives ₹1,06,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Current assets from working capital and current ratio
questions.question: A company's working capital is ₹1,80,000 and its current ratio is 2.5 : 1. Its current assets are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹3,00,000
Step 1: Working capital = CA − CL = 2.5 CL − CL = 1.5 CL = ₹1,80,000 → CL = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Current assets = 2.5 × ₹1,20,000 = ₹3,00,000
Common mistake: ₹1,20,000 (A) is the current liabilities. Multiplying the working capital by 2.5 gives ₹4,50,000 (B). ₹1,80,000 (D) is the working capital.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Interest coverage with debentures and a term loan
questions.question: A company's profit before tax is ₹1,60,000. It has 10% debentures of ₹2,00,000 and a 12% term loan of ₹1,00,000. Its interest coverage ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6 times
Step 1: Interest = 10% × ₹2,00,000 + 12% × ₹1,00,000 = ₹20,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹32,000
Step 2: PBIT = ₹1,60,000 + ₹32,000 = ₹1,92,000
Step 3: Interest coverage = ₹1,92,000 ÷ ₹32,000 = 6 times
Common mistake: Using PBT gives 5 times (B). Considering only the debenture interest gives 9.6 times (C). PBT ÷ debenture interest gives 8 times (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Users of financial statements and the ratios they watch
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (User)
(A) Short-term creditors
(B) Long-term lenders
(C) Equity shareholders
(D) Management

List-II (Main focus)
(I) Liquidity ratios
(II) Solvency ratios
(III) Profitability ratios
(IV) Activity (turnover) ratios, to judge operating efficiency
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Suppliers want to be paid soon → liquidity (I).
(B) Debenture holders and banks care about long-term repayment and interest → solvency (II).
(C) Owners care about returns → profitability (III).
(D) Managers use turnover ratios to check how efficiently resources are used (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps liquidity and solvency; (C) swaps solvency and profitability; (D) swaps liquidity and activity.
Key point: Each user reads the ratios that answer their own question.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Choosing a tool — comparing firms of different sizes
questions.question: An investor wants to compare the cost structure of Firm X (revenue ₹10 crore) with that of Firm Y (revenue ₹2 crore) for the same year. The most suitable tool is:
options: B) Comparative statements of Firm X alone
D) The journal of each firm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Common-size statements
Why: Expressing each item as a percentage of revenue removes the effect of size, so the cost structure of a large and a small firm can be compared directly.
Why not the others:
(B) A comparative statement of one firm shows changes over time, not between firms.
(C) A cash budget is a planning tool.
(D) Journals record transactions; they do not analyse them.
Key point: Inter-firm comparison of different sizes → common-size.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Trade receivables turnover — interpretation
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the trade receivables turnover ratio:
(A) A higher ratio indicates faster collection from customers.
(B) It is based on credit revenue from operations.
(C) Bills receivable are included in trade receivables.
(D) A lower ratio indicates efficient credit management.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The ratio = Credit revenue ÷ Average trade receivables (B), where trade receivables = debtors + bills receivable (C). A higher figure means debts are collected more quickly (A).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — a LOWER ratio means slower collection, which suggests weak credit control. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Higher receivables turnover → shorter collection period → better.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from investing activities — goodwill, patents and investments
questions.question: During the year, a manufacturing company bought goodwill for ₹40,000, sold patents with a book value of ₹15,000 at a profit of ₹5,000, bought long-term investments for ₹30,000 and received interest of ₹3,000 on investments. Net cash flow from investing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹47,000 outflow
Step 1: Outflows: goodwill ₹40,000 + investments ₹30,000 = ₹70,000
Step 2: Inflows: sale of patents ₹15,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹20,000; interest ₹3,000
Step 3: Net = −70,000 + 20,000 + 3,000 = −₹47,000
Common mistake: Taking the patents at book value gives ₹52,000 (B). Ignoring the interest gives ₹50,000 (C). Ignoring the sale of patents gives ₹67,000 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: VLOOKUP nested inside IF
questions.question: An employee table in A2:C4 holds: E101 | Sales | 28,000; E102 | Accounts | 30,500; E103 | HR | 26,000. The formula =IF(VLOOKUP("E102",A2:C4,3,FALSE)>30000,"High","Normal") returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) High
Step 1: VLOOKUP finds E102 and returns its third-column value, 30,500
Step 2: IF tests 30,500 > 30,000 → TRUE → "High"
Common mistake: Reading the row of E101 or E103 gives "Normal" (B). #N/A (C) would appear only if E102 were missing. 30,500 (D) is the inner VLOOKUP result, not the final output.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Keyboard shortcuts in a spreadsheet
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Key)
(A) Ctrl + Z
(B) Ctrl + Y
(C) F2
(D) F4 (while editing a reference)

List-II (Action)
(I) Undo the last action
(II) Redo the last undone action
(III) Edit the active cell
(IV) Toggle between relative and absolute reference
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Ctrl + Z undoes (I).
(B) Ctrl + Y redoes (II).
(C) F2 opens the active cell for editing (III).
(D) F4 cycles a reference through A1 → $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps undo and redo; (B) swaps redo and edit; (C) swaps undo and F4.
Key point: F4 is the quickest way to make a rate cell absolute.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll — leave without pay and PF
questions.question: An employee's monthly salary is ₹31,000 for a 31-day month. She took 3 days' leave without pay, deducted as =B2/31*3. PF is deducted at 12% of the salary actually earned. Her net salary is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹24,640
Step 1: LWP deduction = ₹31,000 ÷ 31 × 3 = ₹3,000 → salary earned = ₹28,000
Step 2: PF = 12% × ₹28,000 = ₹3,360
Step 3: Net = ₹28,000 − ₹3,360 = ₹24,640
Common mistake: Charging PF on the full ₹31,000 gives ₹24,280 (A). Ignoring PF gives ₹28,000 (B). Ignoring the leave deduction gives ₹27,280 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — COUNTIF with a 'not equal to' criterion
questions.question: In a fee register, cells B2:B7 show the status of six students: Paid, Pending, Paid, Waived, Pending, Pending. The formula =COUNTIF(B2:B7,"<>Paid") returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4
Why: The criterion "<>Paid" counts cells NOT equal to 'Paid' — Pending, Waived, Pending, Pending = 4.
Why not the others:
(A) 2 counts 'Paid'.
(B) 6 counts all the cells.
(D) 3 counts only 'Pending'.
Key point: <> means 'not equal to' in a criterion.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Charts — trend over time
questions.question: A finance manager wants to show how the firm's monthly sales moved over the twelve months of a year. The most suitable chart is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Line chart
Why: A line chart joins values in time order, making rises, falls and seasonal patterns easy to see.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) show parts of a whole, not trends.
(C) A single stacked bar shows composition at one point.
Key point: Time series → line chart.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Charts — features
questions.question:
Which of the following statements about spreadsheet charts are correct?
(A) A chart updates automatically when its source data changes.
(B) A chart can be placed on the same worksheet or on a separate chart sheet.
(C) The legend identifies the data series shown.
(D) A pie chart is the best way to show a trend over twelve months.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Charts are linked to their data (A), can be embedded or placed on their own sheet (B), and use a legend to label each series (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — trends over time are best shown by a line or column chart; a pie chart shows parts of one whole. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Choose the chart that matches the question you are answering.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — monthly charge from SLN
questions.question: A laptop costing ₹48,000, with no salvage value and a useful life of 4 years, is depreciated monthly. The schedule uses =SLN(48000,0,4)/12. The monthly depreciation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,000
Step 1: =SLN(48000,0,4) = ₹12,000 a year
Step 2: Monthly = ₹12,000 ÷ 12 = ₹1,000
Common mistake: ₹12,000 (A) is the annual charge. Dividing by 12 months but using a 1-year life gives ₹4,000 (C). Dividing by 144 gives ₹333 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan schedule — interest in the second EMI
questions.question: A loan of ₹1,20,000 at 12% p.a. is repaid in 12 monthly EMIs of ₹10,662. In month 1, interest was ₹1,200 and principal ₹9,462. The interest in month 2 (on the reduced balance) is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,105
Step 1: Balance after month 1 = ₹1,20,000 − ₹9,462 = ₹1,10,538
Step 2: Interest for month 2 = ₹1,10,538 × 1% = ₹1,105 (approx.)
Common mistake: Repeating month 1's interest gives ₹1,200 (A). ₹9,462 (B) is month 1's principal. ₹10,662 (C) is the full EMI.
Key point: In an EMI loan, interest falls and principal rises each month.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — MOD
questions.question: An instalment schedule uses =MOD(25,7) to find how many days are left over after complete weeks in a 25-day period. The formula returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4
Why: MOD returns the REMAINDER after division: 25 ÷ 7 = 3 complete weeks, remainder 4.
Why not the others:
(B) 3 is the quotient (INT(25/7)).
(C) 3.57 is the plain division.
(D) 18 is 25 − 7.
Key point: INT → whole quotient; MOD → remainder.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — saving with a keyboard shortcut
questions.question: The keyboard shortcut commonly used to save the workbook you are working on is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ctrl + S
Why: Ctrl + S saves the current file; saving often protects accounting work from being lost.
Why not the others:
(A) Ctrl + P prints.
(C) Ctrl + Z undoes the last action.
(D) Ctrl + C copies.
Key point: S = Save, P = Print, Z = Undo, C = Copy.
